title: Cisco CCNP Cybersecurity Study Guide
description: CCNP Cybersecurity is Cisco's SOC-operations professional certification — the renamed CyberOps Professional (February 2026): the CBRCOR core plus a forensics or threat-hunting concentration. It's the defender-analyst track: incident response, forensic analysis, and hunting — and it is NOT CCNP Security, which is a different cert about building firewalls. That confusion wastes careers; this guide won't let it.
audience: Working SOC analysts stepping toward senior-analyst, incident-response, and threat-hunting roles — people who already live in SIEMs and want the professional credential for the operations side. Assumes CCNA Cybersecurity-level knowledge (or equivalent SOC experience), not beginner status.
why_get_it: It's the only Cisco professional cert aimed squarely at the SOC chair: CBRCOR covers fundamentals, techniques, processes, and automation of security operations, and the two concentrations certify the highest-value analyst specializations — forensics/IR (CBRFIR) or threat hunting (CBRTHD). Every exam passed earns a standalone Specialist credential. The honest scope note: this track's ecosystem is thinner than CCNP Security's — fewer job postings name it explicitly, and third-party study material is sparse. Its value is strongest for analysts in Cisco-tooling SOCs and as a structured skill ladder; for pure HR-filter power, CySA+ and eventually CISSP still dominate the operations lane. Pair, don't substitute.
when_to_get_it: After a year or two of real SOC work, when CCNA Cybersecurity-level material feels like Monday morning rather than a challenge. The rename matters for your study materials: this was CyberOps Professional until February 3, 2026 — exams and content are unchanged (350-201 CBRCOR, 300-215 CBRFIR, 300-220 CBRTHD), so 'CyberOps Professional' books and courses remain valid; they just wear the old name. And decide the fork honestly first: if what you actually want is to BUILD security infrastructure — firewalls, ISE, VPNs — stop and read our CCNP Security guide instead.
salary_note: No cert-specific salary data exists for this track — anchor to the role instead: BLS puts Information Security Analysts at a $124,910 median (May 2024) — but that category spans the whole security-analyst field and skews above SOC-specific pay. Senior SOC, incident-response, and threat-hunting seats typically land $90–130K in U.S. markets, with federal/cleared work above that. Directional, third-party, and role-driven — the cert signals readiness for the senior tier; it doesn't create it.
exam_format: Two proctored exams at Pearson VUE (test center or OnVUE): the CBRCOR core plus one of two concentrations. Multiple-choice and scenario items; counts and passing scores not published. Results in ~48 hours.

exam_structure.name: Performing Cybersecurity Using Cisco Security Technologies
exam_structure.note: Security-operations fundamentals, techniques, processes, and automation. Earns a Specialist credential on its own. Unchanged by the Feb 2026 rename.

exam_structure.name: Conducting Forensic Analysis and Incident Response Using Cisco Technologies for Cybersecurity
exam_structure.note: The forensics/IR lane — evidence handling, artifact analysis, response process at professional depth.

exam_structure.name: Conducting Threat Hunting and Defending Using Cisco Technologies for Cybersecurity
exam_structure.note: The threat-hunting lane — hypothesis-driven hunting, adversary techniques, detection engineering.

recertification_note: 3-year cycle, 80 CE credits on the unified ledger: CBRCOR re-pass = 80 CE, a concentration = 40, Cisco U training counts, excess rolls over. Taking the second concentration next cycle is the natural renewal — and completes your coverage of both analyst specializations.

items: SOC processes, playbooks, and metrics beyond the tier-1 view
Advanced monitoring: correlating across network, endpoint, and identity telemetry
Risk assessment and asset context in triage decisions
Cisco security stack integration as the SOC sees it
Automation of security operations — SOAR concepts and scripting
Evidence collection and handling that survives scrutiny
Host and memory artifact analysis fundamentals
Malware behavior analysis at the analyst (not reverse-engineer) level
The response lifecycle run properly: contain, eradicate, recover, learn
Writing findings the legal and leadership layers can act on
Hypothesis-driven hunting — starting from adversary behavior, not alerts
MITRE ATT&CK as a working tool rather than a poster
Detection engineering: turning hunt findings into durable coverage
Threat intelligence application at the operational level
The proactive muscle that separates senior analysts from alert-clickers

study_steps.title: Confirm the fork: operations, not engineering
study_steps.description: Thirty seconds that saves a year, in the other direction this time: CCNP Cybersecurity = SOC operations (triage, forensics, hunting). CCNP Security = building the security infrastructure. If firewalls and ISE are the pull, switch guides now. If SIEMs and incidents are home, you're in the right place.

study_steps.title: Use the rename to your advantage when buying materials
study_steps.description: The Feb 2026 rename changed names, not content — so 'CyberOps Professional' and 'CBRCOR' books, courses, and question banks remain fully valid, and some sell at old-name discounts. Third-party material for this track is thin either way; the official CLN exam-topics pages and Cisco U carry most of the load.

study_steps.title: Build CBRCOR on your daily work plus the blueprint
study_steps.description: The core rewards working analysts: map every blueprint topic to something you've actually done, and lab the gaps. Cisco U's paths cover it officially; the free CLN study groups fill the discussion void where Reddit-scale communities don't exist for this track.

study_steps.title: Lab the analyst stack free
study_steps.description: Cisco's free DevNet sandboxes (Secure Firewall, XDR APIs) plus TryHackMe's SOC and DFIR paths give hands-on reps for both concentration lanes. Splunk's free tier and Security Onion round out a zero-cost professional-depth lab.

study_steps.title: Pick the concentration by the chair you want
study_steps.description: CBRFIR if incident response and forensics is the destination — the more common senior-analyst road. CBRTHD if proactive hunting and detection engineering pulls you — rarer skills, increasingly demanded. Either passes alone earns a Specialist credential; the second one makes a natural recert cycle later.

study_steps.title: Sit both exams while momentum holds
study_steps.description: CBRCOR ($400, 120 min), then the concentration ($300, 90 min) — no lab exam at this tier. Results in ~48 hours each. The professional cert completes on the second pass.

study_steps.title: Stack the vendor-neutral layer for the filters
study_steps.description: The blunt truth about the SOC hiring lane: CySA+ and (later) CISSP dominate the HR filters this cert doesn't reach. CCNP Cybersecurity proves professional-depth operations skill; pair it with the neutral credentials that get the resume opened. Our CySA+ and CISSP guides cover both — and the SOC Analyst path shows the whole ladder.

faq.question: CCNP Cybersecurity vs CCNP Security — settle it once.
faq.answer: Different careers wearing similar names. CCNP Cybersecurity (this guide, formerly CyberOps Professional) is the SOC-OPERATIONS track: triage, incident response, forensics, threat hunting — the defender-analyst chair. CCNP Security is the ENGINEERING track: building and running firewalls, ISE, and VPN/SSE. Cisco's February 2026 renames made this collision worse, not better — pick by the chair, not the name.

faq.question: Is my old CyberOps Professional study material still valid?
faq.answer: Yes, fully — the February 2026 change renamed the certification but left exams and content untouched: same 350-201 CBRCOR core, same CBRFIR/CBRTHD concentrations, same blueprints. Books and courses wearing the old name remain accurate; existing CyberOps Professional holders were migrated automatically.

faq.question: Which concentration — forensics or threat hunting?
faq.answer: CBRFIR (forensics/IR) is the more common senior-analyst road and maps to incident-responder roles directly. CBRTHD (threat hunting) certifies rarer, increasingly demanded proactive skills — hypothesis-driven hunting and detection engineering. Honest tiebreaker: pick the one your current SOC actually lets you practice; the other makes a perfect recertification cycle in three years.

faq.question: Does this cert get me past HR filters?
faq.answer: Less than it should, honestly. Fewer postings name it than name CySA+ or CISSP in the operations lane, and its recognition concentrates in Cisco-tooling SOCs. Its real value is professional-depth skill validation and internal advancement. The winning stack for the SOC ladder: CySA+ for the filters, this for the depth, CISSP when the experience years arrive — our SOC Analyst path maps the whole road.

faq.question: How does it renew?
faq.answer: 3-year cycle, 80 CE credits on Cisco's unified ledger — a CBRCOR re-pass covers it alone (80 CE), or take the concentration you skipped (40 CE) plus modest training credits. The two-concentration route has the nice side effect of certifying both analyst specializations.
